title: The generator set in a power system

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the voltage fall at once by the sub-transient reactance's share, then climb back only as the AVR acts, when you press Start.
interactive.title: Starting the big motor
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Fifteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue: six show an idea, nine ask you to try it. No marks, no timers. Each puzzle reads as its question in the read-through.

The picture. Left, one generator set, 630 kVA at 440 V and 60 Hz, feeding a board. A second, identical set is drawn dashed beside it, joined to the board through its breaker only when the Second set switch is on. A motor hangs off the board, behind a starter box marked DOL, Star-delta or Soft starter. Its feeder shows the kVA the sets see, written as the slider writes it, such as 1,200 kVA. A small AVR box sits on the set. Right, two traces against time, 0 to 4 s, with Start at 0 s. Above, the board voltage as a % of 440 V, from 60% to 105%, with a dashed line at 90%. Below, the board frequency, from 50 to 61 Hz, with its lowest point labelled. The motor's shaft turns once it gets away. If it stalls, the motor turns red and is labelled Stalled. On the screens with sets A and B, each set joins the board through its own breaker, both drawn the same.

The controls. A Starting kVA slider, the motor's starting load when started DOL, from 100 to 1,200 kVA in steps of 50, opening at 600 kVA. A Start method choice of three, in this order: DOL, Star-delta, Soft starter, opening on DOL. A Second set switch, opening off. A Start button. It plays the 4 s at half speed, taking 8 s, and pressing it again starts over. Changing any control clears the traces. Four readout tiles, wrapping onto two rows on a phone: At once in %, Lowest in %, Recovers to in %, and Torque in %. The Torque tile shows only for a DOL start. A star-delta or soft start hides it, because the starter itself cuts the motor's torque. At once fills at Start, Lowest at 1 s, and the other two at 3 s. Until then each shows –. The method buttons wrap too, so no word splits.

The rule it computes. The starting kVA the set sees is the slider's figure for DOL, a third of it for Star-delta, and half of it for the Soft starter, an example limit. Divide it by 630 kVA for each set on the board, and call that x. The sub-transient reactance is 0.15 per unit and the synchronous reactance 1.5, example values. At once, the voltage left is 1 ÷ (1 + 0.15 × x). This treats the motor's starting impedance, 1 ÷ x, and the reactance as a divider. Recovered, the voltage is 2.5 ÷ (1 + 1.5 × x), capped at 100%. The 2.5 is E at the AVR's field ceiling, an example. Torque = the recovered voltage squared, as a % of the DOL start's torque on full voltage. The start's real power is the starting kVA × 0.4, an example starting power factor. The frequency dips by 3% for every 100 kW of it, shared between the sets on the board, an example. With t in seconds from Start, the frequency is 60 × (1 − the dip × (t ÷ 0.3) × e^(1 − t ÷ 0.3)), a sketch that is lowest at 0.3 s. The AVR's pull is the recovered voltage − (the recovered voltage − the voltage at once) × e^(−t ÷ 1), a sketch. The voltage drawn is that pull × the frequency ÷ 60, because a slower rotor makes less voltage. Lowest is the voltage trace's lowest point. If the recovered voltage is 90% or more, the motor gets away at 3 s, an example run-up. Its current then falls, and the voltage returns to 100% over 0.5 s. Below 90%, the voltage stays down, and at 2 s the motor turns red, stalled. The 90% line promises enough torque for most loads, not all, so the words say the motor stalls with this load. The sentence under the picture changes only at 1 s, 2 s and 3 s of the run, so each holds for at least 2 s as it plays.

The blackout picture, screen 12. No traces or tiles. Sets A and B, each behind its own breaker, on a board drawn dashed and labelled dead in red. Three loads, 1, 2 and 3, each behind a breaker, labelled loads, in steps. Start plays it at half speed. Both sets start at 0.4 s, reading starting. Both breakers close at 1.4 s, the board turns solid and reads live, and each set reads on the board. The loads' breakers close at 2.4, 3.0 and 3.6 s, and each load box fills. It is a sequence, not drawn to time.

Screen 1, try it, a recall, picked. No picture. "A motor takes 100 A at full load. Started direct on line, roughly what current does it draw at first?" Three options: About 100 A, 600 to 800 A, About 200 A. Answer 600 to 800 A (a range, so picked, not typed). About 100 A: "That is its running current. A start draws several times more." About 200 A: "That is nearer a star-delta start, about a third of DOL." Hint when wrong: "A DOL start usually draws 6 to 8 times full-load current." Why: "6 to 8 × 100 A gives 600 to 800 A, so about 700 A. The current stays high until the motor reaches about 75% of its speed.[^1]" A right Check shows "Still there."

Screen 2, show. One set, DOL, 600 kVA, the traces empty until Start. The words build the divider. A load drawing the set's own 630 kVA at full voltage is 1 per unit, and a bigger load a smaller impedance. So the motor is 630 ÷ 600 = 1.05 per unit, and 1.05 ÷ (1.05 + 0.15) = 87.5% is left. They end "Press Start to watch the drop.", left out of the read-through. Still: the traces drawn to 0.05 s, At once 87.5%, the others –.

Screen 3, try it, a prediction. One set, DOL, 600 kVA, before Start, the AVR box lit. "The AVR is on and watching the voltage. The motor is about to start. What does the AVR do to that first drop?" Three choices, in this order: "It stops it, so the voltage holds at 100%"; "Nothing at first, then it pulls the voltage back"; "It makes it deeper, by cutting the field". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The AVR acts only once it sees the voltage fall. The drop comes first."; for the third: "When the voltage falls, the AVR raises the field." Why: "The AVR must see the drop before it acts. Then the field takes time to grow. So a sudden step drops the voltage as far as it would with no AVR at all.[^2]" A right Check runs the start.

Screen 4, show. One set, DOL, 600 kVA, the run free. The words: the start takes 240 kW at 0.4, so the engine slows. A slower rotor makes less voltage,[^3] so the dip deepens to 83.8%. The governor and the AVR bring it back to 100%. Still: the run finished, frequency lowest 55.7 Hz, readouts 87.5%, 83.8%, 100%, 100%.

Screen 5, try it, typed. One set, DOL, 900 kVA, before Start, the feeder reading 900 kVA and the At once tile reading ? until Check. "The same 630 kVA set has a sub-transient reactance of 0.15 per unit. A bigger motor starts DOL and takes 900 kVA. What voltage is left at the first instant, in %, to one decimal place?" A field in %. Answer 82.4%. Slips: 78.6, "That takes the whole 0.15 × 900 ÷ 630 off. The motor's impedance shares the voltage too."; 17.6, "That is the drop. The question asks what is left."; 85, "That leaves out the motor's size." Hint when wrong: "The motor's impedance is 630 ÷ 900 = 0.70 per unit." Why: "0.70 ÷ (0.70 + 0.15) = 0.824, so 82.4% is left." A right Check runs the start.

Screen 6, show. One set, DOL, 900 kVA, the run free. The words: torque goes with voltage squared, so 90% voltage gives 81% torque, enough for most loads.[^4] The reactance grows towards the synchronous 1.5, and the field ceiling is an example E of 2.5. At 900 kVA the same divider gives 2.5 × 0.70 ÷ (0.70 + 1.5) = 79.5%. With this load, the motor stalls. Still: the motor red and Stalled, readouts 82.4%, 72.8%, 79.5%, 63.3%.

Screen 7, try it, typed. No picture. "A start recovers the voltage to only 85%. What torque does the motor make, as a % of its full-voltage torque?" A field in %. Answer 72.3%. Also accepted: 72.25%, 72%. Slips: 85, "Torque goes with the square of the voltage."; 92.2, "That is the square root. Square it instead."; 81, "81% goes with 90% voltage. This voltage is lower." Hint when wrong: "Write the voltage as a fraction, then square it." Why: "0.85 × 0.85 = 0.7225, about 72.3%. That is under the 81% that goes with a 90% recovery."

Screen 8, show. One set, 600 kVA, the Start method free, opening on Soft starter, the run free. The words: star-delta takes 200 kVA and leaves 95.5%. The soft starter, an example half, takes 300 kVA and leaves 93.3%. Both cut the motor's starting torque, so they suit light-starting loads. They end "Switch the start method to compare.", left out of the read-through. Still: readouts 93.3%, 91.4%, 100%, the Torque tile hidden.

Screen 9, try it, typed. One set, Star-delta, 1,200 kVA, before Start, the feeder reading ? kVA and the At once tile reading ? until Check. "The biggest motor here takes 1,200 kVA started DOL. On one set, it is started star-delta instead. What voltage is left at the first instant, in %, to one decimal place?" A field in %. Answer 91.3%. Slips: 77.8, "That is the DOL start. Star-delta draws about a third."; 90.5, "That takes the whole share off. The motor's impedance shares the voltage too."; 8.7, "That is the drop. The question asks what is left." Hint when wrong: "Star-delta's starting load is 1,200 ÷ 3 = 400 kVA." Why: "The motor's impedance is 630 ÷ 400 = 1.575 per unit. 1.575 ÷ (1.575 + 0.15) = 0.913, so 91.3% is left. It recovers to 100%, and the motor gets away." A right Check shows the feeder's 400 kVA and runs the start.

Screen 10, show. DOL, 600 kVA, the Second set switch on, the run free. The words: two sets halve the reactance, so 600 kVA leaves 93.3%, as if each set carried 300 kVA. The drop is 6.7%, not 12.5%, and the frequency dips less. A power management system can hold a big start. Starting loads one at a time keeps each step small, and three motors started one after another can need 40% less starting kW. Still: two sets, readouts 93.3%, 91.4%, 100%, 100%.

Screen 11, try it, typed (mixed). One set, DOL, 900 kVA, the Second set switch off, the At once tile reading ? until Check. "A 900 kVA DOL start stalls on one set. So you synchronise a second, identical set onto the board first. What voltage is left at the first instant now, in %, to one decimal place?" A field in %. Answer 90.3%. Slips: 82.4, "That is one set. Two sets halve the reactance."; 91.2, "Halving the reactance does not quite halve the drop. Work the divider."; 9.7, "That is the drop. The question asks what is left." Hint when wrong: "With two sets, the reactance is 0.15 ÷ 2 = 0.075 per unit." Why: "The motor's impedance is 630 ÷ 900 = 0.70. 0.70 ÷ (0.70 + 0.075) = 0.903, so 90.3% is left. It recovers to 100%, and the motor gets away." A right Check turns the Second set switch on and runs the start.

Screen 12, show. The blackout picture, the run free. The words: a blackout is the whole board lost. The power management system sheds loads and holds big starts to prevent one. If the board still goes dead, it starts the standby sets and closes them onto the dead board.[^5] Several sets can be on, in parallel, within about 15 seconds. Then the loads come back in small steps. They end "Press Start to watch a recovery.", left out of the read-through. Still: the sequence finished, both sets and all three loads on a live board.

Screen 13, try it (mixed). No traces. Set A on the board, set B drawn dashed beside it with its breaker open, labelled not on the board. "After a blackout, set A closes onto the dead board alone and takes the first loads. Set B is now up to speed. What must happen before B's breaker closes?" Three choices, in this order: "Nothing more: B can close at once, as A did"; "B must match the live board in voltage, frequency, phase sequence and angle"; "A must trip first, so that B also closes onto a dead board". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "A closed onto a dead board, with nothing to match. B now faces a live one."; for the third: "Tripping A would black out the board again." Why: "A dead board has no voltage to match, so A could close at once. Once A is on, the board is live. So B is synchronised like any set joining a live board."

Screen 14, try it, typed (mixed). The frequency trace alone, for a 900 kVA DOL start on one set, the frequency lowest reading ? until Check. "A motor's start takes 900 kVA at a power factor of 0.4. How many kW must the engine find at once?" A field in kW. Answer 360 kW. Slips: 900, "That is the kVA. The engine supplies only the kW."; 720, "0.8 is the set's rated power factor. A starting motor's is lower, here 0.4."; 540, "That is the part left over. Multiply by 0.4." Hint when wrong: "kW = kVA × power factor." Why: "900 × 0.4 = 360 kW. The governor needs a moment to add that much fuel, so the frequency dips." A right Check shows the lowest, 53.5 Hz.

Screen 15, try it (mixed). No traces. Two sets drawn on the board, A and B, each through its own closed breaker. "Two sets share the board in droop. Set A's governor fails and drives its fuel up. What happens?" Three choices, in this order: "Only A speeds up, and B carries on as before"; "A takes kW from B, the frequency rises, and B may be driven as a motor"; "The board's voltage rises, but the kW split stays the same". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "A is locked in step with the board. It cannot speed up alone."; for the third: "Fuel moves kW, not voltage." Why: "In parallel, more fuel on A moves kW onto A and off B. The board's frequency rises along the droop lines. If A pushes past the whole load, it drives B as a motor. B's reverse-power relay then trips it. A governor fault at one set reaches the whole board." A right Check shows: "One board, every set."
interactive.ignores: Time on the traces runs at half speed. The divider treats the motor's starting impedance as if it were pure reactance, like the set's. A real one is partly resistive, so the true drop is a little smaller. The move from the sub-transient to the synchronous reactance is drawn as one smooth pull. A real set passes through its transient reactance on the way. The AVR's pull, the engine's slowing and the run-up are sketches with example figures. The torque readout is for a DOL start only. Whether a motor really gets away depends on its load's torque, not on one 90% line. The set carries no other load before the start. The blackout recovery is a sequence, not drawn to time.

explain.text:
A big motor's start is a sudden, heavy load. A generator set feels it at once. The voltage drops before the AVR can move. The engine slows and deepens the dip. Then the governor and the AVR pull the board back. Whether the motor gets away depends on how far the voltage recovers. So big loads are started softly, one at a time, or with more sets on.

Start with the first instant. A DOL start draws about six times the motor's full-load current. It keeps drawing it until the motor reaches about 75% of its speed.[^1] Say the start takes 600 kVA from a 630 kVA set. For the first few cycles, only the set's small sub-transient reactance holds that current back. Take it as 0.15 per unit, the same figure used for fault currents. On the set's own base, the motor's starting impedance is 630 ÷ 600 = 1.05 per unit. In a simplified picture, the two share the voltage like a divider. The motor gets 1.05 ÷ (1.05 + 0.15) = 87.5%. That is a [[voltage dip]] of 12.5%. The AVR cannot stop this. It acts only once it sees the voltage fall. Then the field takes time to grow. So a sudden step drops the voltage as far as it would with no AVR at all.[^2]

Then two things pull in opposite directions. The start also takes 240 kW of real power, at a starting power factor of 0.4. The engine cannot find that at once, so it slows, as with any load step. A slower rotor makes less voltage, so the dip goes deeper.[^3] Meanwhile the governor adds fuel and the AVR raises the field. After the first cycles, the bigger synchronous reactance carries the current. So how far the voltage recovers depends on how much field the AVR can give. A motor's torque goes with the square of its voltage. If the voltage recovers to 90%, the motor makes 81% of its torque, enough to accelerate most loads.[^4] Any less, and it may stall.

So every cure cuts the [[starting kVA]] each set has to carry. Star-delta draws about a third. A soft starter holds the current to a limit. A second set on the board halves the reactance the motor sees. Then the same 600 kVA start leaves 93.3%. Starting loads one after another, not together, keeps each step small. A [[power management system]] can hold a big start until enough sets are on. If the board is lost all the same, it starts the standby sets, closes them onto the dead board and brings the loads back in steps.[^5] These figures come from a simplified picture with example reactances. Real dips also depend on the motor, the AVR and the engine. In parallel, fuel and field share the steady load between the sets. Neither acts fast enough to catch a sudden step. So enough sets must be on before the step comes. **A big motor's start dips a set's voltage before the AVR can act, so big loads start softly, one at a time, or with more sets on.**

analogy.text: Think of a big motor starting at the end of a long, thin sub-main. The cable's impedance and the motor's starting impedance share the supply voltage. So the lights on that board dip. A bigger cable shrinks the dip. So does a second feed in parallel, or a soft start. A set at the first instant behaves the same way, with its sub-transient reactance in place of the cable.
analogy.breaks: A cable's impedance stays the same. A set's grows from the sub-transient to the synchronous reactance as the start goes on. Meanwhile the AVR raises the field to fight it. A cable also has no engine to slow down. So it has no frequency dip.

practice.text:
**Starting a big motor on generator sets**

The safe way first. Start big loads under your procedures, with the board's interlocks in place. Never override a power management system's hold on a start.

- Before a big start, check how many sets are on and how much spare kW they have.
- If another set is needed, start it and synchronise it first. Let the sets share the load before the start.
- Start loads one at a time. Let the voltage and frequency settle between starts.
- Use the starter fitted. A star-delta or soft starter is there to cut the starting current.
- Watch the voltmeter and frequency meter during the start. If the voltage does not recover, or the motor does not run up, stop and find out why.

**Rules of thumb:** voltage left at once ≈ 1 ÷ (1 + sub-transient reactance × starting kVA ÷ set kVA), in per unit. Two equal sets in parallel halve the reactance the motor sees. Torque goes with voltage squared. So 90% voltage gives 81% torque.[^4] Star-delta draws about a third of the DOL starting current.

**Worked example:** a 630 kVA set has a sub-transient reactance of 0.15. A pump motor takes 900 kVA starting DOL. Alone, the first instant leaves 1 ÷ (1 + 0.15 × 900 ÷ 630) = 82.4%. Take a synchronous reactance of 1.5 and a field ceiling of E = 2.5, both example values. Then it recovers to 2.5 ÷ (1 + 1.5 × 900 ÷ 630) = 79.5%. That is under 90%, so the motor may stall. Started star-delta, it takes 300 kVA. That leaves 93.3% at once, and the voltage recovers fully. Started DOL with a second set on, it leaves 90.3% at once and recovers fully.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting the AVR to stop the dip. It can only pull the voltage back after the drop.[^2]
- Judging a start by its kW alone. A motor's start is mostly kVA, at a low power factor.
- Starting several big loads together after a blackout. One at a time keeps each step small.
- Thinking a governor or AVR fault at one set stays there. In parallel, it moves kW or kVAr onto or off the other sets.
